content_preview.title: Rust Team Member's Four Merged PRs Cut Rustdoc Build Times 33%, Landing in Rust 1.99
content_preview.summary: A Rustdoc team member traced a Crater-flagged regression to an expensive impl-inlining pass and shipped four PRs averaging a 33% speedup.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Rustdoc, the tool behind `cargo doc` that generates the Rust standard library docs and the pages hosted on docs.rs, is roughly a third faster after a series of four pull requests merged into `rust-lang/rust` in July. Rustdoc team member Noah Lev Bartell-Mangel wrote in [a blog post](https://noahlev.org/blog/2026/08/27/making-rustdoc-faster/) that the changes produced "an average wall-time reduction of 25% (which is a 33% speedup), with up to 40% on some real-world crates like hyper ...

No suspicious_patterns flagged on any source. Read all 6 in full: source-0.html.gz (noahlev.org blog, the primary source) — every direct quote in the article ('an average wall-time reduction of 25% (which is a 33% speedup)', 'up to 40% on some real-world crates like hyper and bitmaps, and up to 60% on microbenchmarks like helloworld', 'will land on stable in Rust 1.99', 'Last month, Rust release team member @theemathas posted on the Rustdoc Zulip about a strange regression in our latest beta', the Crater/indented-blocks/core::fmt stack-frame quote, the algorithm-complexity quote, the notable-trait/Deref-chain paraphrase, and the closing 'Just because a piece of code... has been a certain way for a long time doesn't mean that it's optimal or even correct' quote) traced verbatim to the post text; author identified in the post itself as 'a member of the Rustdoc team' and named 'Noah Lev Bartell-Mangel' in the byline, matching the article's attribution. source-1.html.gz (GitHub PR #159623): title 'rustdoc: Only build extern trait impls if needed', author camelid, merged by rust-bors into rust-lang:main Jul 22, 2026, milestone 1.99.0 — all match the article. PR description quote 'Building inlined impls is expensive, and most of them end up being unneeded and stripped later in this function. So we should filter them ahead of time.' verified verbatim. source-2.html.gz (PR #159721): 'rustdoc: Only inline impls for local primitives', camelid, merged Jul 23, 2026; quote 'Since most crates do not define #[doc(primitive)]s, this is a bunch of wasted work that is done in every crate.' verified verbatim. source-3.html.gz (PR #159779): 'rustdoc: Only synthesize auto/blanket impls for documented items', camelid, merged Jul 24, 2026; quote 'would skip synthesizing impls if the trait was not documented, but it would still synthesize even if the type was not documented. This is wasted work.' verified verbatim (source italicizes 'trait'/'type', immaterial to the text match). source-4.html.gz (PR #159854): 'rustdoc: Only analyze head of self type when deciding impl inlining', camelid, merged Jul 29, 2026; quote 'We only care about whether the self type is a generic or an item (inlined) in the current crate, so we don't actually need to compute the param_env, which is expensive when done to every external impl.' verified verbatim. source-5.html.gz (github.com/camelid profile): bio reads 'Rust Compiler and Rustdoc team member. PLASMA @ UMass. Compiler enthusiast.' and the display name is 'Noah Lev' — corroborates the article's author attribution and its own in-body citation of the profile.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: All four PR numbers (159623, 159721, 159779, 159854), their exact merge dates (Jul 22/23/24/29, 2026), and every per-PR percentage figure (20% wall-time / 12% max-RSS for #159623; 12% wall-time / 6% max-RSS for #159721; 6% average / up to 13% on hyper for #159779; 18% average for #159854) trace verbatim to the blog post and are internally consistent with it. The headline's 33% figure and its '25% wall-time reduction = 33% speedup' framing is the blog's own verbatim claim, including the author's own published correction explaining the 25%-to-33% math (1/0.75 = 1.333). The rustc-perf CI numbers visible on the PR #159623 page (e.g. -10.8% primary instruction count, -10.9% primary max-RSS) are a separate compiler-perf benchmark suite from the blog author's own Rustdoc benchmark suite (20% wall-time / 12% max-RSS) — the article correctly attributes its percentages to the blog post only and does not conflate the two measurement systems.
